Series::diagonal¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series::diagonal() const -> Series
Series::diagonal(std::int64_t diagonal) const -> Series
Series::diagonal(std::int64_t diagonal, std::int64_t dim1, std::int64_t dim2) const -> Series

What It Does¶

diagonal() always extracts. Unlike diag(), it never switches into matrix-building mode.

That makes it the better root method when you want your call site to state “read a diagonal” unambiguously, regardless of what rank the input happens to be.

The current verified root surface is narrower than the name might suggest:

  • it is currently implemented for 2D inputs

  • the three-argument overload accepts only the two real matrix axes

  • swapping dim1 and dim2 changes which direction the diagonal is read from

Overload Map¶

diagonal()

Extract the main diagonal.

diagonal(std::int64_t diagonal)

Extract an offset diagonal.

diagonal(std::int64_t diagonal, std::int64_t dim1, std::int64_t dim2)

Extract an offset diagonal while naming the two participating axes explicitly.

Parameters¶

diagonal (std::int64_t)

The diagonal offset.

  • 0 selects the main diagonal

  • positive values move toward later columns

  • negative values move toward later rows

dim1 (std::int64_t)

The first matrix axis.

dim2 (std::int64_t)

The second matrix axis.

Both dimension parameters accept negative indexing, but they must refer to two different axes after normalization.

On the current verified root surface, the practical choices for a 2D matrix are just:

  • (0, 1)

  • (1, 0)

The first reads the diagonal in the ordinary orientation. The second reads the diagonal after the matrix axes have been conceptually swapped.

Returns¶

Series A 1D Series containing the extracted diagonal values.

Gradient¶

diagonal() shares the same verified extraction route as matrix-extract diag().

That means reverse-mode sensitivity is scattered back onto the selected diagonal positions and leaves every non-participating position untouched.

Examples¶

Example 1. The zero-argument form extracts the main diagonal.

auto square = pluss::make_series({
    {1, 2, 3},
    {4, 5, 6},
    {7, 8, 9},
}, pluss::ScalarType::Int64);

std::cout << square.diagonal();

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=int64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[1, 5, 9]

Example 2. A positive offset reads above the main diagonal.

auto rectangular = pluss::make_series({
    {1, 2, 3},
    {4, 5, 6},
}, pluss::ScalarType::Int64);

std::cout << rectangular.diagonal(1);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=int64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[2, 6]

Example 3. Swapping dim1 and dim2 changes which matrix orientation is used before the diagonal is read.

std::cout << rectangular.diagonal(0, 1, 0);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=int64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[1, 5]

That result comes from reading the diagonal of the transposed orientation, not from the ordinary (0, 1) orientation.

Example 4. The named axes must differ.

try {
  std::cout << square.diagonal(0, 0, 0) << "\n";
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  std::string msg = e.what();
  std::cout << msg.substr(0, msg.find('\n'));
}

Output¶

diagonal: dim1 and dim2 must differ

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • diagonal() always extracts. If you wanted a diagonal matrix, use diag_embed() or diagflat() instead.

  • The current root surface is 2D-only.

  • Swapping dim1 and dim2 is not cosmetic. It changes the extraction orientation.

  • Reverse-mode follows the same diagonal-scatter rule as matrix-extract diag().

Summary¶

Use diagonal() when you want extraction-only semantics with no ambiguity about embedding. It is the clearer choice whenever input rank should not change the meaning of the call.

  • Series::trace: diagonal extraction followed by reduction.
